title: SQL/JSON path and JSON_TABLE (PG 17)
summary: SQL/JSON path (PG 12) walks and filters inside a document: [*], ? (@ ...), $variables, lax or strict. PG 17's JSON_TABLE turns a document into typed rows, with NESTED PATH for child arrays, and JSON_VALUE, JSON_QUERY and JSON_EXISTS extract with explicit ON EMPTY and ON ERROR behaviour.

examples.title: jsonpath: filters, variables, @?, and lax vs strict mode

annotations.note: Read the path left to right: $ is the document, .suites[*] every suite, .tests[*] every test, ? (...) keeps the tests whose status is "failed", .title takes their title. jsonb_path_query is set-returning: one output row per match, so report 2, with no failure, has no row at all. The values are jsonb, hence "Çıkış" in quotes.

$max is a path variable, supplied as a jsonb object: the jsonpath form of a bind parameter, so no value is spliced into the path text. Report 2's "slow" is a string, "slow" > 500 is unknown in SQL/JSON's three-valued logic, and the filter drops the test without a word.
@? asks "does the path return anything?". Together with @@ (for predicates such as '$.build > 100') it is the form a GIN index on report can serve; the path functions are not.
size() counts array elements: 2 and 1. Lax mode makes an exception for size() and type() and doesn't unwrap the array first; otherwise size() would run on each suite object and return 1.
No [*] anywhere: in lax mode an accessor applied to an array is applied to each element. Convenient, and also why a lax path accepts data shaped differently from what you expected.
Lax mode also suppresses the missing-key error. Only Çıkış has an error key; the other tests contribute nothing.

SQLSTATE 2203A. strict mode raises structural errors, here a test without an error key, instead of skipping them. Use it when the document has a contract; for optional keys in strict mode, filter with exists (@.error) first.

examples.title: JSON_TABLE: one row per test, NESTED PATH, and an import that fails loudly

annotations.note: JSON_TABLE (PG 17) sits in FROM and is joined laterally to each ci_reports row, so it can read r.report. The row path $.suites[*] makes one row per suite.
FOR ORDINALITY numbers the rows from 1. Each NESTED PATH has its own counter, so test_no restarts in every suite; together they keep the document's order as data.
NESTED PATH makes child rows joined to their parent: one row per test, suite columns repeated. export has no tests and still appears once, with NULL test columns, as a LEFT JOIN would show it.
In report 2, Giriş's "slow" and Çıkış's missing ms both come out NULL: a column defaults to NULL ON EMPTY and NULL ON ERROR, so a type error and an absent value look the same.
An EXISTS column is true when its path finds anything: a cheap "has an error" flag that doesn't extract the value.
For loading, the row path starts at $ to pick up build once, then nests suites and tests. The JSON_TABLE output feeds INSERT ... SELECT directly: the document becomes rows in one statement.
DEFAULT 0 ON EMPTY fills a missing ms; ERROR ON ERROR turns "slow" into SQLSTATE 22P02, and the whole INSERT fails instead of storing a silent NULL. A failed import is better than a wrong dashboard.

examples.title: JSON_VALUE, JSON_QUERY, JSON_EXISTS: RETURNING, PASSING, ON EMPTY, ON ERROR

annotations.note: JSON_VALUE returns one scalar, as text unless RETURNING names a type: the JSON string "108" becomes the integer 108.
RETURNING timestamptz parses the ISO 8601 string. The Z (UTC) instant is displayed in the session's time zone: 09:12+03.

ON EMPTY applies only when the path finds nothing: report 2 has no owner and gets 'nobody'. Report 1's owner is JSON null, which is an item; JSON_VALUE turns it into SQL NULL and the default isn't used.
JSON_QUERY returns JSON. A path that yields several items needs WITH WRAPPER to collect them into an array; without it, several items are an error, and errors become NULL by default.
PASSING binds the SQL value 500 to $max: the standard spelling of the vars argument in example 1.
ON ERROR and ON EMPTY default to NULL, so "more than one value", "not a scalar" and "not there" are three different problems with the same answer.
SQLSTATE 22034 names the actual problem. Wherever a NULL would be stored or displayed as if it were data, ask for ERROR ON ERROR.

use_cases: Importing JSON exports and API responses into tables with one INSERT ... SELECT ... FROM JSON_TABLE
Questions about nested arrays without unnesting by hand: failed tests inside suites inside a CI report
Parameterized filters over stored payloads: tests slower than $max, events of a given type
Typed extraction with validation in a staging step: JSON_VALUE ... RETURNING date ERROR ON ERROR
strengths: One path expression replaces chains of ->, jsonb_array_elements and LATERAL joins for nested arrays
JSON_TABLE yields typed columns and ordinality, so a document becomes rows that join, group and insert like any table
Path variables ($max, PASSING) keep values out of the path text, as bind parameters do for SQL
Per column or call you choose what missing or malformed data means (NULL, DEFAULT, ERROR), which is more control than a JSON decoder's all-or-nothing
weaknesses: Lax mode and the NULL defaults hide malformed data: a misspelled key or a string where a number belongs simply disappears
jsonpath is a second language inside SQL, with its own syntax (==, &&, like_regex), its own three-valued logic and its own case rules
JSON_TABLE and the SQL/JSON query functions need PostgreSQL 17; older servers need jsonb_array_elements and LATERAL for the same job
Index support comes only through operators (@?, @@, @>, ?); the path functions and JSON_TABLE in a WHERE clause read every document

pitfalls.title: Using lax mode as validation
pitfalls.detail: Lax paths unwrap arrays and skip missing keys, so a document of the wrong shape returns less data instead of an error. Use strict mode, or ERROR ON ERROR, where shape matters.

pitfalls.title: Building a path from user input
pitfalls.detail: Concatenating a value into the path lets the value change the path's structure (a quote ends the string literal). Pass it as a variable.

pitfalls.title: JSON_TABLE columns that swallow errors
pitfalls.detail: By default a wrong type becomes NULL, indistinguishable from a missing value. Say ERROR ON ERROR on required columns of an import.
pitfalls.good: ms int PATH '$.ms' DEFAULT 0 ON EMPTY ERROR ON ERROR

pitfalls.title: jsonb_path_query in the SELECT list drops rows
pitfalls.detail: It is set-returning: a document with no match produces no row at all. Use jsonb_path_query_array or jsonb_path_query_first to keep one row per document.

pitfalls.title: Case-insensitive like_regex and Turkish letters
pitfalls.detail: flag "i" pairs letters by the database's default collation, not Turkish rules; under StackLab's builtin C.UTF-8 locale that is Unicode's simple case mapping. On StackLab's PostgreSQL 18.7, '^izmir' with flag "i" matches IZMIR but not İzmir, and '^ığdır' matches Iğdır. For Turkish case-insensitive search, extract the text and use the search module's ICU tools.

quiz.q: In lax mode, what does `$.suites.tests.title` return for {"suites": [{"tests": [{"title": "A"}]}]}?
quiz.why: In lax mode an accessor applied to an array is applied to each of its elements; strict mode would raise an error instead.

quiz.q: A JSON_TABLE column `ms int PATH '$.ms'` meets "ms": "slow". What happens by default?
quiz.why: Column-level ON ERROR defaults to NULL; ERROR ON ERROR makes it fail with SQLSTATE 22P02.

quiz.q: The report has "owner": null. What does `JSON_VALUE(report, '$.owner' DEFAULT 'nobody' ON EMPTY)` return?
quiz.why: The path found an item, the JSON null, so the result isn't empty; JSON_VALUE returns SQL NULL for a JSON null.

quiz.q: Why pass `'{"max": 500}'` as the vars argument instead of concatenating 500 into the path?
options: The value can't change the path's structure: it is the jsonpath form of a bind parameter
quiz.why: Variables are values, never syntax, exactly like $1 in a prepared SQL statement.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: The SQL/JSON Path Language
PostgreSQL docs: Strict and Lax Modes

body:
## Concept

The operators from the previous lesson address one value at a time. For nested arrays
("every failed test in every suite") and for turning documents into rows, PostgreSQL
implements two layers of the SQL standard.

**SQL/JSON path** (PG 12) is a small language, passed as a `jsonpath` value, that
addresses items inside one document: `$` is the document, `.key` a member, `[n]` and
`[*]` array elements, `? (condition)` a filter in which `@` is the item being tested,
`$name` a variable, and methods such as `.size()`, `.type()` and `.datetime()`. A path
runs in **lax** mode (the default: arrays are unwrapped automatically, structural errors
such as missing keys are suppressed) or **strict** mode (they are raised). The functions
are `jsonb_path_query` (one row per item), `jsonb_path_query_array`,
`jsonb_path_query_first`, `jsonb_path_exists` and `jsonb_path_match`, plus the
operators `@?` and `@@`.

**SQL/JSON query functions** (PG 17) use the same paths with standard syntax and
explicit error handling:

- `JSON_VALUE` extracts one scalar and casts it with `RETURNING`.
- `JSON_QUERY` extracts JSON (`WITH WRAPPER` collects several items into an array).
- `JSON_EXISTS` tests whether the path finds anything.
- `JSON_TABLE` turns a document into rows: a row path, typed columns with their own
  paths, `FOR ORDINALITY`, `EXISTS` columns, and `NESTED PATH` for child arrays.

Each of them lets you choose what happens `ON EMPTY` (the path found nothing) and `ON
ERROR` (wrong type, several items where one was expected, a structural error in strict
mode): `NULL` (the default for values), `DEFAULT expr`, or `ERROR`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **TypeScript/JS:** the path in example 1 is
  `report.suites.flatMap(s => s.tests).filter(t => t.status === 'failed').map(t => t.title)`.
  `JSON_TABLE` is what you'd do with zod and a loop: parse, check each field's type,
  emit rows. The difference is the default: zod throws on a bad field, `JSON_TABLE`
  quietly writes NULL until you say `ERROR ON ERROR`.
- **Python:** `pandas.json_normalize(report, record_path=['suites', 'tests'],
  meta=['build'])` is `JSON_TABLE` with nested paths.
- **Go:** `encoding/json` decoding "slow" into an `int` field reports an
  `UnmarshalTypeError`. `ERROR ON ERROR` gives you that strictness inside SQL; the default
  is more lenient than Go.
- **XML users:** jsonpath plays the role of XPath, and `JSON_TABLE` is the JSON
  counterpart of `XMLTABLE`, which PostgreSQL also has.

## How it works

`JSON_TABLE` behaves like a set-returning function in `FROM`: it is evaluated for each
row of the tables before it, which is why it can read `r.report` without the `LATERAL`
keyword. The row path produces parent rows; each `NESTED PATH` produces child rows that
are joined to their parent, and a parent without children is kept with NULL child
columns. Sibling `NESTED PATH`s at the same level are combined with `UNION`, not
multiplied.

In a filter, comparisons follow SQL/JSON's three-valued logic: comparing a string with a
number yields *unknown*, and the filter keeps only items for which the condition is
true. That is how report 2's `"ms": "slow"` vanished from example 1 without an error.

## Design notes

Use `JSON_TABLE` at the boundary. When a document arrives (an import, a webhook, an
export from another system), turn it into rows once and work relationally from there.
Per column, decide the contract: required fields get `ERROR ON EMPTY ERROR ON ERROR`,
optional ones `DEFAULT ... ON EMPTY`. A parent without children still yields one row
with NULL child columns, so an import of tests should filter `WHERE title IS NOT NULL`
or treat that row deliberately.

Prefer strict mode or explicit `ERROR ON ERROR` where the document has a contract; keep
lax mode for exploring heterogeneous data. Pass values as variables, never by string
concatenation.

For filters on stored documents that must be fast, write them with `@?`, `@@` or `@>`,
which a GIN index can serve (next lesson). The path functions and `JSON_TABLE` in a
`WHERE` clause read every document.

Case-insensitive `like_regex` (flag "i") folds case through the database's default
collation: the source compiles the regex with it (src/backend/utils/adt/jsonpath_exec.c,
function executeLikeRegex). StackLab's database uses the builtin `C.UTF-8` locale, whose
case mapping the docs (Locale Support) call the "simple" variant, and the regex engine
applies it per character (src/backend/regex/regc_pg_locale.c, pg_wc_tolower and
pg_wc_toupper): a lower-case i in the pattern matches i and I, never İ, and ı matches I.
Observed on PostgreSQL 18.7: '^izmir' matched izmir and IZMIR but not İzmir, '^ığdır'
matched ığdır, Iğdır and IĞDIR. Another database may have another default collation:
`datlocprovider` in `pg_database` names the provider, and `datlocale` (for libc,
`datctype`) the locale.

files.examples/01_jsonpath.sql:
-- LEARN(sql.json.path-table): a jsonpath walks, filters and unwraps inside one document.
CREATE TABLE ci_reports (
  id     int   PRIMARY KEY,
  report jsonb NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO ci_reports VALUES
  (1, '{"build": 108, "suites": [
         {"name": "auth", "tests": [
            {"title": "Giriş", "status": "passed", "ms": 120},
            {"title": "Çıkış", "status": "failed", "ms": 85, "error": "timeout"}]},
         {"name": "export", "tests": [
            {"title": "CSV dışa aktarım", "status": "passed", "ms": 900}]}]}'),
  (2, '{"build": 109, "suites": [
         {"name": "auth", "tests": [
            {"title": "Giriş", "status": "passed", "ms": "slow"}]}]}');

-- [*] iterates an array, ? (...) filters, @ is the item being tested.
-- jsonb_path_query returns one row per match; report 2 has none.
SELECT id,
       jsonb_path_query(report, '$.suites[*].tests[*] ? (@.status == "failed").title')
         AS failed
FROM ci_reports
ORDER BY id;

-- Collect matches as an array, pass values in as variables, test with @?.
SELECT id,
       jsonb_path_query_array(report, '$.suites[*].tests[*].title') AS titles,
       jsonb_path_query_array(report, '$.suites[*].tests[*] ? (@.ms > $max).title',
                              '{"max": 500}')                       AS slow,
       report @? '$.suites[*].tests[*] ? (@.status == "failed")'   AS any_failed,
       jsonb_path_query_first(report, '$.suites.size()')             AS suites
FROM ci_reports
ORDER BY id;

-- lax mode (the default) unwraps arrays without [*] and skips missing keys.
SELECT id,
       jsonb_path_query_array(report, '$.suites.tests.title') AS unwrapped,
       jsonb_path_query_array(report, '$.suites.tests.error') AS errors
FROM ci_reports
ORDER BY id;

-- strict mode treats a missing key as an error.
SELECT jsonb_path_query_array(report, 'strict $.suites[*].tests[*].error')
FROM ci_reports
WHERE id = 1;
files.examples/02_json_table.sql:
CREATE TABLE ci_reports (
  id     int   PRIMARY KEY,
  report jsonb NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO ci_reports VALUES
  (1, '{"build": 108, "suites": [
         {"name": "auth", "tests": [
            {"title": "Giriş", "status": "passed", "ms": 120},
            {"title": "Çıkış", "status": "failed", "ms": 85, "error": "timeout"}]},
         {"name": "export", "tests": []}]}'),
  (2, '{"build": 109, "suites": [
         {"name": "auth", "tests": [
            {"title": "Giriş", "status": "passed", "ms": "slow"},
            {"title": "Çıkış", "status": "passed"}]}]}');

-- One row per test: the row path picks the suites, NESTED PATH the tests
-- inside each suite, and every column has its own path and SQL type.
SELECT r.id, jt.*
FROM ci_reports AS r,
     JSON_TABLE(r.report, '$.suites[*]' COLUMNS (
       suite_no  FOR ORDINALITY,
       suite     text PATH '$.name',
       NESTED PATH '$.tests[*]' COLUMNS (
         test_no   FOR ORDINALITY,
         title     text PATH '$.title',
         ms        int  PATH '$.ms',
         has_error boolean EXISTS PATH '$.error'))) AS jt
ORDER BY r.id, jt.suite_no, jt.test_no;

-- For an import, be explicit: a missing ms gets a default, a wrong type fails.
CREATE TABLE test_results (build int, suite text, title text, ms int);
INSERT INTO test_results
SELECT jt.*
FROM ci_reports AS r,
     JSON_TABLE(r.report, '$' COLUMNS (
       build int PATH '$.build',
       NESTED PATH '$.suites[*]' COLUMNS (
         suite text PATH '$.name',
         NESTED PATH '$.tests[*]' COLUMNS (
           title text PATH '$.title',
           ms    int  PATH '$.ms' DEFAULT 0 ON EMPTY ERROR ON ERROR)))) AS jt;
files.examples/03_query_functions.sql:
SET TimeZone = 'Europe/Istanbul';

CREATE TABLE ci_reports (
  id     int   PRIMARY KEY,
  report jsonb NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO ci_reports VALUES
  (1, '{"build": "108", "finished": "2026-11-13T06:12:00Z",
        "suites": [{"name": "auth", "slowest_ms": 120},
                   {"name": "export", "slowest_ms": 900}],
        "owner": null}'),
  (2, '{"build": "109", "suites": [{"name": "auth", "slowest_ms": 130}]}');

-- JSON_VALUE extracts one scalar and casts it with RETURNING; JSON_QUERY
-- returns JSON; JSON_EXISTS tests. PASSING binds path variables.
SELECT id,
       JSON_VALUE(report, '$.build' RETURNING int)               AS build,
       JSON_VALUE(report, '$.finished' RETURNING timestamptz)    AS finished,
       JSON_VALUE(report, '$.owner' DEFAULT 'nobody' ON EMPTY)   AS owner,
       JSON_QUERY(report, '$.suites[*].name' WITH WRAPPER)       AS suites,
       JSON_EXISTS(report, '$.suites[*] ? (@.slowest_ms > $max)'
                   PASSING 500 AS max)                           AS has_slow
FROM ci_reports
ORDER BY id;

-- By default every problem becomes NULL: two values where one was expected,
-- an object instead of a scalar, a missing key.
SELECT JSON_VALUE(report, '$.suites[*].name') AS two_values,
       JSON_VALUE(report, '$.suites[0]')      AS an_object,
       JSON_VALUE(report, '$.nope')           AS missing
FROM ci_reports
WHERE id = 1;

-- Ask for errors where a NULL would hide a bug.
SELECT JSON_VALUE(report, '$.suites[*].name' ERROR ON ERROR)
FROM ci_reports
WHERE id = 1;
